chapters.1: Jeremiah describes his call as a young man to be God's prophet to the nations, even though he protests he is too young to speak. God reassures him of his support and gives him two visions, an almond branch showing God will quickly fulfill his word, and a boiling pot tipping from the north, warning that a northern invader (Babylon) will bring judgment on Judah for its idolatry.
chapters.2: God recalls Israel's early devotion to him like a young bride, then accuses the nation of abandoning him, 'the fountain of living waters,' for worthless idols, comparing this to digging broken cisterns that can't hold water. He condemns their wandering after other nations like Egypt and Assyria for help and compares their erratic unfaithfulness to a wild animal in heat, saying their own actions, not God, have brought their coming suffering.
chapters.3: Using the imagery of adultery and divorce, God describes Israel's unfaithfulness as worse than any human marriage breakdown, noting that even seeing her sister-nation Judah's similar betrayal didn't stop Judah from also being unfaithful. Despite this, God offers to take back his 'backsliding' people if they will simply acknowledge their guilt and return to him, and envisions a future reunited Israel and Judah worshiping together in Jerusalem.
chapters.4: Jeremiah urges the people to truly repent ('circumcise yourselves to the Lord') rather than simply go through outward motions, warning that a terrifying invading army, pictured as a roaring lion from the north, is coming as judgment. He conveys deep personal anguish over the coming destruction, describing a vision of the land reduced to chaos and emptiness, and depicts Jerusalem's coming suffering like a woman in labor pains.
chapters.5: God sends Jeremiah to search Jerusalem for even one honest, righteous person, but finds none among rich or poor, since the people have abandoned justice and truth and chase after false gods and adultery. As punishment, he announces that a powerful foreign nation will come and devastate their harvests and cities, blaming corrupt prophets, priests, and the people's own willful blindness for the coming disaster.
chapters.6: God calls for the people of Jerusalem to flee as a destroying army from the north approaches to besiege the city as punishment for widespread violence and dishonesty. He criticizes the prophets and priests for falsely reassuring the people with 'peace, peace' when there is no real peace, and compares the testing of the nation to refining metal that produces no good result because the wicked refuse to be purified.
chapters.7: Standing at the temple gate, Jeremiah delivers a sermon warning that simply having the temple ('the temple of the Lord') will not protect the people if they keep oppressing others and worshiping idols, citing the earlier destruction of Shiloh as a precedent. He describes disturbing idolatrous practices, including child sacrifice at Topheth, and tells Jeremiah not even to bother praying for the people since judgment is now certain.
chapters.8: Jeremiah describes a coming disaster so severe that even bones will be dug up from graves, and laments that the people stubbornly refuse to turn back to God despite clear warnings, unlike migratory birds that instinctively know their proper season. He grieves deeply over the nation's coming collapse, famously asking, 'Is there no balm in Gilead?' as he mourns that there seems to be no cure for his people's wound.
chapters.9: Jeremiah weeps over the deceit and betrayal that have corrupted relationships throughout society, where even friends and family can't be trusted to tell the truth. God announces that because of their persistent unfaithfulness, he will scatter the people among foreign nations and turn their land into desolation, calling for professional mourners to grieve the coming devastation and reminding the people that true pride should come only from truly knowing God.
chapters.10: Jeremiah mocks the foolishness of idol worship, describing man-made idols as lifeless objects that must be carried around and nailed down so they don't fall over, compared to the true, living God who made the heavens and earth. He laments the coming devastation of the land and prays for correction tempered with justice rather than full-force anger, asking God to direct his fury instead toward the hostile nations.
chapters.11: God reminds Jeremiah of the covenant he made with Israel's ancestors and announces that because the people have repeatedly broken it by worshiping Baal, disaster is now unavoidable and even their prayers for help will go unanswered. The chapter closes with Jeremiah learning that his own hometown of Anathoth is plotting to kill him for his prophecies, and God promises to punish them for it.
chapters.12: Jeremiah questions God about why wicked people seem to prosper, and God responds by warning Jeremiah that even harder trials lie ahead for him. God laments that Judah, his own 'inheritance,' has become hostile to him and will be devastated by enemies, but promises that afterward he will have compassion and eventually restore the people and even surrounding nations if they turn to him.
chapters.13: God tells Jeremiah to bury a linen belt by the Euphrates and later dig it up ruined, symbolizing how God will ruin the pride of Judah and Jerusalem because of their stubborn disobedience. He also uses the image of wine jars filled with drunkenness and pleads with the people to humble themselves before darkness falls, warning that their deep-rooted sinfulness (like a leopard's spots) makes their coming judgment inevitable.
chapters.14: This chapter describes a severe drought afflicting Judah, prompting Jeremiah to pray earnestly on the people's behalf despite their sins. God responds that the false prophets reassuring the people with promises of peace are lying, and that judgment by sword, famine, and plague is still coming, even as Jeremiah continues pleading passionately for mercy on the nation's behalf.
chapters.15: God tells Jeremiah that the nation's judgment is now fixed and unavoidable, even on the appeal of figures like Moses or Samuel, largely due to the sins committed under King Manasseh. Jeremiah complains bitterly about the burden and hostility his prophetic calling brings him, and God both reaffirms his difficult mission and promises to protect and sustain him through it.
chapters.16: God tells Jeremiah, as a living sign to the people, not to marry or have children, and not to mourn the dead or celebrate at feasts, illustrating how normal life is about to be disrupted by coming disaster. Despite this bleak announcement of exile and judgment, the chapter ends with a promise that God will eventually bring the people back from the lands where they're scattered, and that even foreign nations will one day recognize the true God.
chapters.17: Jeremiah contrasts the person who trusts in merely human strength, who will wither like a desert shrub, with the person who trusts in God, who will flourish like a tree planted by water. He prays for healing and vindication against his enemies, and the chapter closes with a call to properly observe the Sabbath, warning that Jerusalem's future depends on this simple act of obedience.
chapters.18: God sends Jeremiah to watch a potter reworking a flawed piece of clay, illustrating that nations, like clay, can still be reshaped by repentance or ruined by continued disobedience. When the message to repent is relayed, the people refuse, responding by plotting against Jeremiah himself, which leads Jeremiah to pray for God's protection and justice against his conspirators.
chapters.19: God instructs Jeremiah to smash a clay jar in front of the elders and priests as a dramatic symbol that Jerusalem and its people will be shattered beyond repair because of their idolatry, including child sacrifice in the valley of Hinnom (Topheth). Jeremiah then delivers this same stark warning of coming destruction publicly at the temple.
chapters.20: After the priest Pashur has Jeremiah beaten and put in stocks for his prophecies, Jeremiah predicts Pashur's own downfall and captivity in Babylon. Jeremiah then pours out raw, personal anguish to God over the suffering and ridicule his prophetic mission brings him, even briefly cursing the day he was born, showing just how heavy this calling weighs on him.
chapters.21: King Zedekiah sends officials to ask Jeremiah to seek God's help against the besieging Babylonian army, but Jeremiah responds that God himself will fight against Jerusalem and hand it over to Babylon. He tells the people that whoever stays in the besieged city will die, but whoever surrenders to the Babylonians will survive, and warns the royal house to act justly or face fiery judgment.
chapters.22: Jeremiah delivers warnings to Judah's royal house, urging justice and condemning the exploitation of workers and the vanity of building luxurious palaces unjustly. He pronounces specific judgments on several kings, including Shallum (Jehoahaz), Jehoiakim (who will be denied proper burial), and Jehoiachin/Coniah (who will be exiled and whose line will not successfully retain the throne).
chapters.23: God condemns the corrupt 'shepherds' (leaders) who have scattered his people, but promises to one day gather the remnant and raise up a righteous ruler from David's line, called 'the Lord our righteousness.' He strongly denounces the false prophets who prophesy comforting lies without God's authority, declaring that their false promises of peace will ultimately be shown empty.
chapters.24: God shows Jeremiah a vision of two baskets of figs, one good and one spoiled, symbolizing two groups: the exiles already taken to Babylon, whom God will treat with mercy and eventually restore, and those remaining in Judah under Zedekiah, who will face further disaster. The vision reframes exile as something God intends for the eventual good of those taken.
chapters.25: After twenty-three years of warnings that the people have ignored, Jeremiah announces that Babylon will overrun Judah and the surrounding nations, who will serve Babylon for seventy years before Babylon itself is punished in turn. Using the image of a 'cup of God's wrath,' Jeremiah symbolically makes many nations 'drink' this judgment, declaring that God's judgment is spreading from nation to nation across the whole earth.
chapters.26: Jeremiah publicly warns at the temple that Jerusalem will be destroyed like Shiloh if the people don't repent, which provokes priests and prophets to demand his execution for this unpopular message. Jeremiah defends himself by insisting God sent him, and the officials and elders ultimately spare his life, recalling that a past king didn't kill the prophet Micah for a similar message, though another prophet named Urijah is not so fortunate and is executed.
chapters.27: God tells Jeremiah to wear a wooden yoke and send word to surrounding kings and to Judah's own King Zedekiah that they must submit to Babylon's rule, since God has given Nebuchadnezzar authority over the region for a time. He specifically warns against trusting prophets who claim the exile will be short or that the temple's valuables will soon return, since these are false promises.
chapters.28: The prophet Hananiah publicly contradicts Jeremiah, breaking his symbolic yoke and falsely declaring that Babylon's domination will end within two years. Jeremiah responds that true prophecy is proven by what actually happens, and Hananiah dies within the year exactly as Jeremiah then predicts, for leading the people to trust a lie.
chapters.29: Jeremiah sends a letter to the Jews already exiled in Babylon, telling them to settle down, build normal lives, and even pray for the peace of Babylon rather than expecting a quick return, since the exile will last seventy years. He reassures them that God still has good plans for their future ('plans to give you hope'), while condemning false prophets among the exiles, like Ahab, Zedekiah, and Shemaiah, who deceive the people with false promises of a swift return.
chapters.30: God promises through Jeremiah that despite the severe coming 'time of Jacob's trouble,' he will ultimately rescue and restore both Israel and Judah, breaking the yoke of foreign oppression and bringing them back to their land. He acknowledges that Israel's wound is self-inflicted through sin, but promises genuine healing and restoration once his purifying judgment is complete.
chapters.31: This chapter is full of hope, promising that God will regather and restore scattered Israel with joy, turning mourning into dancing and comforting even Rachel's symbolic weeping for her lost children. It contains the famous promise of a 'new covenant' in which God's law will be written directly on people's hearts, offering complete forgiveness rather than external rules, and ends affirming that Israel's restoration is as certain as the fixed laws of nature.
chapters.32: While Jerusalem is under siege and Jeremiah is imprisoned for his unpopular prophecies, God tells him to buy a field from his cousin as a symbolic act of hope, showing that normal life (buying and owning property) will one day resume in the land. Jeremiah prays acknowledging God's power and Judah's deserved punishment, and God responds by reaffirming that after judgment, he will indeed restore the people, land, and ordinary life there.
chapters.33: God promises Jeremiah, still imprisoned, that Jerusalem's ruins will be healed and restored, with joy and normal life (marriages, worship) returning to its empty streets. He reaffirms the promise of a righteous future ruler from David's line ('the Lord our righteousness') and declares his commitment to David's dynasty and the priesthood is as unbreakable as the fixed cycle of day and night.
chapters.34: As Babylon besieges Jerusalem, God warns King Zedekiah through Jeremiah that the city will fall and he personally will be captured, though he'll die peacefully rather than violently. Jeremiah also condemns the people for freeing Hebrew slaves as required by law during the crisis, then quickly forcing them back into slavery once pressure eased, declaring that this broken promise will bring its own judgment.
chapters.35: Jeremiah uses the Rechabites, a group who have faithfully kept their ancestor's command to avoid wine and live simply for generations, as an object lesson, contrasting their consistent obedience with Judah's repeated disobedience to God despite generations of prophetic warnings. God promises to bless the faithful Rechabites while confirming judgment on unfaithful Judah.
chapters.36: God instructs Jeremiah to have his scribe Baruch write down all his prophecies in a scroll, which is read publicly and eventually brought before King Jehoiakim, who defiantly burns it piece by piece in the fire. Undeterred, Jeremiah has Baruch rewrite the scroll with the same words plus more, while God pronounces specific judgment on Jehoiakim for destroying it.
chapters.37: During Zedekiah's reign, as Babylon's siege is briefly lifted due to an advancing Egyptian army, Jeremiah warns that the Babylonians will certainly return and conquer the city regardless. Jeremiah is then falsely accused of deserting to the enemy and imprisoned, though King Zedekiah secretly has him moved to better conditions in the court of the prison.
chapters.38: Jeremiah is thrown into a muddy cistern for his unpopular warnings but is rescued by a compassionate official named Ebed-melech before he dies. King Zedekiah secretly consults Jeremiah again, who urges him to surrender to Babylon to save his life and the city, but Zedekiah, fearing backlash, refuses to act on this advice.
chapters.39: This chapter narrates the actual fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, including Zedekiah's capture, the killing of his sons before his eyes, his own blinding, and the city and temple being burned. Amid the devastation, God specifically protects both Jeremiah and the official Ebed-melech, who had earlier shown kindness and faith.
chapters.40: After the fall of Jerusalem, Jeremiah is freed from captivity and chooses to remain in Judah under the newly appointed governor Gedaliah rather than go to Babylon. Many scattered Jews return to settle under Gedaliah's leadership, but the chapter ends with an ominous warning that a man named Ishmael is plotting to assassinate Gedaliah, a plot Gedaliah refuses to believe.
chapters.41: Ishmael, acting on behalf of a hostile king, assassinates the Judean governor Gedaliah and massacres many people at Mizpah, including innocent pilgrims, throwing bodies into a pit. He then takes captives and flees, but Johanan and other officers pursue him, rescue most of the captives, and the group ends up fearfully preparing to flee toward Egypt.
chapters.42: The remaining Judean leaders ask Jeremiah to seek God's guidance about whether to flee to Egypt, promising in advance to obey whatever answer comes. God's answer, delivered through Jeremiah, is clear: stay in the land and he will protect them, but if they go to Egypt instead, the very disasters (sword, famine) they fear will catch up with them there.
chapters.43: Despite God's clear warning, the people accuse Jeremiah of lying and forcibly take him, Baruch, and the remaining community down into Egypt anyway. Once there, Jeremiah symbolically buries large stones at the entrance of Pharaoh's palace, predicting that Babylon's king will one day conquer Egypt too, setting his throne on that very spot.
chapters.44: Jeremiah confronts the Jewish refugees in Egypt for continuing the same idolatry (worshiping 'the queen of heaven') that caused Jerusalem's destruction, but the people stubbornly insist on continuing their practices, blaming hardship on having stopped them earlier. Jeremiah responds that this community in Egypt will also be judged, with only a small remnant surviving, and gives as a confirming sign that Egypt's own Pharaoh will be overthrown by his enemies.
chapters.45: This short, personal chapter contains God's response to Jeremiah's scribe Baruch, who had despaired over the hardships of recording Jeremiah's difficult prophecies. God acknowledges the coming widespread devastation but promises Baruch personally that his life will be spared through it all.
chapters.46: This chapter begins a series of oracles against foreign nations, opening with a vivid prophecy of Egypt's military defeat by Babylon at Carchemish, describing Egypt's proud army collapsing in panicked retreat. It closes with a brief, contrasting reassurance to Israel that even while Egypt and other nations face judgment, God will eventually restore and protect his own people.
chapters.47: This short oracle announces judgment against the Philistines, describing an invading force from the north sweeping over their land like a flood and leaving cities like Gaza and Ashkelon devastated and mourning. It closes by acknowledging that this destruction comes as a deliberate command from God, not random chance.
chapters.48: This lengthy oracle pronounces extensive judgment on Moab for its pride and false confidence in its own wealth and security, describing city after city being destroyed and its people fleeing in grief. Despite the thoroughness of the judgment, the chapter ends with an unexpected promise that God will eventually restore Moab's fortunes in the future.
chapters.49: This chapter contains shorter judgment oracles against several nations: Ammon (punished for seizing Israelite territory, though later restored), Edom (judged for pride despite its rocky, seemingly secure strongholds), Damascus/Syria, the Arab tribes of Kedar and Hazor, and Elam (scattered to the four winds, but likewise eventually restored). Each oracle describes the nation's downfall at the hands of invaders sent by God.
chapters.50: This chapter begins an extended judgment oracle against Babylon itself, predicting its complete downfall at the hands of a northern invading force (the Medes and allied nations) as payback for its cruelty toward Israel. Amid Babylon's foretold destruction, God promises that Israel and Judah will be gathered back to their own land and their guilt pardoned.
chapters.51: This long chapter continues and intensifies the prophecy against Babylon, describing in detail its coming total destruction as God's instrument of vengeance for what it did to Jerusalem and the Jewish exiles. The chapter closes with Jeremiah instructing an official named Seraiah to read this prophecy aloud in Babylon itself and then sink the scroll in the Euphrates River as a symbolic sign that Babylon will sink and never rise again.
chapters.52: This closing historical chapter recounts the fall of Jerusalem in detail: Zedekiah's capture and blinding, the burning of the temple and city, the destruction of the temple's bronze furnishings, and the numbers of people taken into Babylonian exile. It ends on a small note of hope, describing how years later the exiled King Jehoiachin is treated kindly and given a regular place at the Babylonian king's table for the rest of his life.
